rubric_bfs_q1.question_text: Explain Breadth First Search (BFS) algorithm and state its time and space complexity.
rubric_bfs_q1.model_answer: Breadth First Search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that begins at a source node and explores all immediate neighbors at the current depth level before moving on to vertices at the next depth level. It utilizes a Queue (FIFO) data structure to keep track of discovered vertices and a boolean visited array to prevent cycles. In an unweighted graph, BFS computes the shortest path from a source. Its time complexity is O(V + E) where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges, and auxiliary space is O(V) for the queue.

rubric_30533f67.question_text: Explain QuickSort partition procedure and worst-case complexity.
rubric_30533f67.model_answer: QuickSort chooses a pivot and partitions the array such that elements smaller than pivot are on the left and larger on the right. Worst-case is O(n^2) when array is already sorted.

sheet_demo_01.raw_ocr_text: Breadth First Search (BFS) is a fundamental graph traversal algorithm. It starts from a chosen root/source node and explores all neighboring vertices at the current depth level before proceeding to vertices at the next depth level. Key Characteristics: 1. Data Structure Used: It uses a Queue (First-In, First-Out / FIFO) to manage vertices that have been discovered but not fully processed. 2. Visited Array: Maintains a boolean array to track visited vertices and prevent loops. 3. Application: BFS reliably computes the single-source shortest path in unweighted graphs. Complexities: - Time Complexity: O(V + E) where V is total vertices and E is total edges. - Auxiliary Space: O(V) for queue storage in worst case.
